tips.body: $\sin = \frac{O}{H}$, $\cos = \frac{A}{H}$, $\tan = \frac{O}{A}$. **Label the sides first** — opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse — then pick the ratio that uses the two sides you care about and ignore the third.

tips.title: Label from the angle, not from the page
tips.body: **Opposite** and **adjacent** swap over depending on which angle you are working from. The **hypotenuse** never moves — it is always opposite the right angle. Label the hypotenuse first, then the opposite, and whatever is left is the adjacent.

tips.title: Finding an angle means an inverse
tips.body: If the **angle** is missing, use $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$ — the **shift** key on the calculator. Pressing plain $\sin$ on a ratio gives a meaningless number, which is the usual sign this step was missed.

tips.title: Is the answer a sensible size?
tips.body: The **hypotenuse must be the longest side**, and an angle in a right-angled triangle must be **under 90°**. If a side comes out longer than the hypotenuse, the ratio was used upside down.

tips.title: Is the unknown on the top or the bottom?
tips.body: If the unknown is on **top**, multiply: $O = H \sin\theta$. If it is on the **bottom**, divide: $H = \frac{O}{\sin\theta}$. Multiplying when you should divide is the most common slip, and it always makes the answer too small.

steps.title: Labelling the sides
steps.body:
**In a right-angled triangle, the three sides are named relative to the angle you are working from.**

- **Hypotenuse** — opposite the **right angle**. Always the longest side, and it **never changes**.
- **Opposite** — opposite the **angle you are using**.
- **Adjacent** — the remaining side, next to the angle.

**Label the hypotenuse first.** It is fixed, so it is the safe starting point. Then find the angle in question, look straight across from it for the **opposite**, and whatever side is left is the **adjacent**.

**Opposite and adjacent swap when you change angle.** A triangle has two acute angles, and a side that is opposite one of them is adjacent to the other. That is not a trick — it is the definition — but it is where most labelling errors come from.

The three ratios are

$$\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H} \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{A}{H} \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$$

remembered as **SOH CAH TOA**.

**Choosing a ratio is mechanical**: mark the side you know and the side you want, then pick the ratio that contains both. The third side is irrelevant, and you never need it.

steps.title: Finding a side
steps.body:
**Label, choose the ratio, then look at where the unknown sits.**

- Unknown on **top** → **multiply**.
- Unknown on the **bottom** → **divide**.

That single distinction accounts for most of the marks lost on this topic, and it is worth writing the rearranged formula down before reaching for the calculator.

**Make sure the calculator is in degrees.** A calculator in radians gives wrong answers that look entirely plausible, with no error message.

steps.title: Why the ratios work at all
steps.body:
**All right-angled triangles with the same angles are similar**, so their sides are in the same proportion however big they are. That is the whole reason a single number like $\sin 35°$ can be useful — it is a **ratio**, and ratios do not care about size.

**A triangle proves it.** Take the 3, 4, 5 triangle and find the angle opposite the side of 3 using each ratio in turn:

- $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = 36.87°$
- $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) = 36.87°$
- $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = 36.87°$

All three agree, because they describe the **same** angle from different pairs of sides. Any ratio you have the two sides for will do — so **choose the one using the sides you were given**, not the one you remember best.

**Which explains a common piece of advice**: prefer the sides the question actually supplies over a side you worked out yourself. If your earlier answer was wrong, using it again carries the error forward; using the **given** sides keeps each part independent.

**Two useful sanity checks fall out of the definitions.**

- $\sin$ and $\cos$ are always **less than 1**, because the hypotenuse is the longest side and it is on the bottom. A ratio above 1 means the fraction was inverted.
- $\tan$ has **no such limit** — it passes 1 at 45° and grows without bound — because both sides in it are shorter sides.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Label before you choose.** Hypotenuse first, because it is fixed by the **right angle**; then opposite, looking across from the angle in question; then adjacent, which is whatever remains. Opposite and adjacent **swap** if you switch to the other acute angle, and that swap is behind most wrong-ratio answers.

**Top or bottom decides multiply or divide.** With the unknown on **top**, multiply: $O = H\sin\theta$. With it on the **bottom**, divide: $H = \frac{O}{\sin\theta}$. Multiplying when you should divide always makes the answer **too small**, and if the result is smaller than a side it should exceed, that is the error.

**Finding an angle needs an inverse.** $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$ — the shift key. An "angle" of 0.38 is the signature of pressing plain $\sin$ on a ratio.

**Check the calculator is in degrees.** Radians produce wrong answers with no warning and no error message. It is worth confirming before the first question of a paper, not after.

**Sine and cosine can never exceed 1**, since the hypotenuse sits underneath and is the longest side. A value above 1 means the fraction is upside down. **Tangent has no such limit**, because it uses the two shorter sides — it reaches 1 at 45° and grows from there.

**Prefer the sides you were given.** Any ratio containing your two known sides gives the same angle, so pick the one built from the **question's** numbers rather than from a value you worked out in an earlier part. If that earlier answer was wrong, reusing it carries the mistake forward; using the given sides keeps the parts independent.

**Round only at the end, and only as asked.** Carry the full value through every intermediate step. Rounding an angle to 1 decimal place and then using it to find a side introduces an error the mark scheme will not allow.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Hypotenuse**: opposite the **right angle**, always longest, **never changes**.
- **Opposite**: across from the angle you are using. **Adjacent**: the side left over.
- Opposite and adjacent **swap** if you work from the other acute angle.
- **SOH CAH TOA**: $\sin = \frac{O}{H}$, $\cos = \frac{A}{H}$, $\tan = \frac{O}{A}$.
- Choose the ratio containing the side you **know** and the side you **want**.
- Unknown on **top** → **multiply**. Unknown on the **bottom** → **divide**.
- Multiplying instead of dividing always makes the answer **too small**.
- Finding an **angle** needs an **inverse**: $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$, via **shift**.
- An "angle" like 0.38 means plain sine was pressed instead of the inverse.
- Check the calculator is in **degrees**; radians fail silently.
- $\sin$ and $\cos$ are **never above 1**; a larger value means an inverted fraction.
- $\tan$ has **no upper limit**, passing 1 at 45°.
- All three ratios give the **same angle**, so use the sides the question **gave you**.
- The hypotenuse must be the **longest** side, and each other angle **under 90°**.
- **Round once, at the end** — never round an angle and then use it.

questions.prompt: Explain how to label the sides of a right-angled triangle, how to choose which trigonometric ratio to use, and how to decide whether to multiply or divide.
questions.solution:
The three sides are named **relative to the angle being used**, so labelling has to come first.

Start with the **hypotenuse**, because it is the only one that is fixed: it is the side **opposite the right angle**, and it is always the longest. It does not change no matter which acute angle you work from, which makes it the safe place to begin.

Then find the angle the question is about and look **straight across** from it — that side is the **opposite**. Whatever side remains is the **adjacent**, the one lying alongside the angle.

An important consequence: **opposite and adjacent swap over** if you switch to the other acute angle, because a side opposite one acute angle is adjacent to the other. The hypotenuse stays where it is. Forgetting to relabel when moving between parts of a question is a very common source of wrong-ratio answers.

The three ratios are remembered as **SOH CAH TOA**:

$$\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H} \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{A}{H} \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$$

**Choosing between them is mechanical.** Mark the side you **know** and the side you **want**, then pick the ratio containing **both**. The third side plays no part and never needs to be found. For a known hypotenuse and a wanted opposite, that is $\sin$; for two shorter sides, $\tan$, which avoids the hypotenuse entirely.

The last decision is **multiply or divide**, and it depends on where the unknown sits in the fraction.

If the unknown is on **top**, multiply. From $\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}$ with $H$ known, $O = H\sin\theta$. With a hypotenuse of 12 and an angle of 35°, $O = 12\sin 35° = 6.88$.

If the unknown is on the **bottom**, divide. With the opposite known and the hypotenuse wanted, $H = \frac{O}{\sin\theta}$. With an opposite of 9 and an angle of 40°, $H = \frac{9}{\sin 40°} = 14.00$.

Getting this the wrong way round always makes the answer **too small**, and it is easy to catch: here, multiplying would have given about 5.79, which is shorter than the 9 cm opposite side and so impossible, since the hypotenuse must be the longest side.

Finally, if the **angle** is what is missing rather than a side, form the ratio from the two known sides and undo it with an **inverse** function — $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$, reached with the shift key.

questions.prompt: A ladder 6 m long rests against a vertical wall with its foot 1.5 m from the base of the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground and how far up the wall it reaches, explaining your choice of method and how you check each answer.
questions.solution:
The **right angle** in this situation is between the **wall and the ground**, since the wall is vertical. The **ladder** lies opposite that right angle, so the ladder is the **hypotenuse**, 6 m. Reasoning from the right angle rather than from which line looks slanted is what makes this reliable.

Relative to the angle at the ground, the 1.5 m along the ground is the **adjacent** side, and the height up the wall is the **opposite**.

**The angle.** I know the adjacent (1.5) and the hypotenuse (6), so I use **CAH**:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{1.5}{6} = 0.25$$

The angle is missing, so I undo the cosine with the **inverse**:

$$\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.25) = 75.5°$$

**The height.** I could use $\sin$ with the angle I have just found, but it is better to use the sides the **question** gave me. Pythagoras does exactly that:

$$h = \sqrt{6^2 - 1.5^2} = \sqrt{36 - 2.25} = \sqrt{33.75} = 5.81 \text{ m (2 d.p.)}$$

The reason for preferring this is that it keeps the two answers **independent**. If my angle were wrong, using it to find the height would carry that error forward and lose marks twice over. Working from the original 6 m and 1.5 m means a mistake in one part cannot contaminate the other.

**Checking both answers.**

The angle is **75.5°**, which is under 90° as any angle in a right-angled triangle other than the right angle must be. It is also a large angle, which fits: the foot is only 1.5 m out from a 6 m ladder, so the ladder is steep. Had I found something like 14°, that would describe a ladder lying almost flat and would not match the numbers.

The height is **5.81 m**, comfortably **less than the 6 m ladder**, as it has to be — a ladder cannot reach higher than its own length. If it had come out above 6 m, I would know the ratio had been used upside down or Pythagoras applied the wrong way round.

As a further confirmation, running the trigonometry forwards gives $6\cos 75.5° = 1.50$ m, recovering the distance along the ground that the question started with.

examTechnique.body:
**Label first**: hypotenuse (opposite the right angle), then opposite, then adjacent. Mark what you **know** and what you **want**, and pick the ratio holding both.

Then ask where the unknown sits: on **top**, multiply; on the **bottom**, divide. If the **angle** is missing, use the **inverse** — and check the calculator is in degrees.
examinerErrors: Multiplying when the unknown was on the bottom of the fraction.
Pressing $\sin$ rather than $\sin^{-1}$ when finding an angle.
Keeping the old labels after switching to the other acute angle.
Leaving the calculator in radians, which fails silently.
Accepting a sine or cosine above 1 instead of spotting an inverted fraction.
Giving a side longer than the hypotenuse.
Reusing a rounded answer from an earlier part instead of the given sides.
Rounding an angle and then using it to calculate a side.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer **labels the triangle before choosing a ratio**, starting from the right angle, and relabels when the angle changes. It says whether the unknown is on the **top or the bottom** before calculating, and writes the rearranged formula down. It uses an **inverse** for a missing angle, and it sanity-checks: sine and cosine never exceed 1, no side exceeds the hypotenuse, and every other angle is under 90°. In a multi-part question it works from the **given** sides rather than its own earlier answer, and it carries full values through, rounding **once** at the end.
